text:
A Florida man pleaded guilty today to a $42 million fraud on Medicare involving false claims for durable medical equipment (DME) and cancer genetic testing. He also pled guilty to fraudulently obtaining a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan.

According to court documents and statements made in court, Chad Monroe, 48, of Tarpon Springs, Florida, conspired with others to submit fraudulent claims for DME — such as knee, wrist, ankle, and back braces — and cancer genetic testing that Medicare beneficiaries did not want or need. Monroe and his co-conspirators opened three DME companies, Maksix Medical Products Inc., Orthotech Atlanta, LLC, and 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC, which they used to submit over $26 million in false and fraudulent claims to Medicare, Medicare Advantage plans, and TRICARE.

Monroe directed co-conspirators to lie on Medicare enrollment documents to hide Monroe’s ownership of and role at the companies. To generate the doctors’ orders for DME and genetic testing, Monroe paid purported telemedicine companies’ illegal kickbacks. Monroe, through his company Health and Life Networking LLC, sold the doctors’ orders for genetic testing to co-conspirator laboratories, which paid him over $15 million in illegal kickbacks.

Monroe also directed a co-conspirator to submit a fraudulent PPP loan for over $30,000 in which he and his co-conspirator lied about, among other things, the ownership of 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC to qualify for the loan.

Monroe used the proceeds of the fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, including by purchasing a 47-foot yacht valued at over $600,000 called “The Rogue Shark,” a Cadillac Escalade, and other luxury vehicles. In connection with the charges, the government seized the yacht and more than $1 million.

Monroe pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and one count of wire fraud. A sentencing date has not been set. He faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison on the health care fraud conspiracy and 30 years in prison on the wire fraud charge. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Inspector General (HHS-OIG) Special Agent in Charge Isaac M. Bledsoe; Special Agent in Charge Rodney Crawford of the FBI Tampa Field Office; Department of War Office of Inspector General’s Defense Criminal Investigative Services (DCIS) Acting Special Agent in Charge Nakia M. Alexander of the DCIS Southeast Field Office; and Acting Special Agent in Charge Charles Miller of the IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) Florida Field Office made the announcement.

HHS-OIG, FBI, DCIS, and IRS-CI investigated the case.

Assistant Deputy Chief Catherine Wagner, Deputy Chief D. Keith Clouser, and Trial Attorney Paul J. Koob of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Health Care Fraud Section are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

text:
By MOAA Staff

The House passed the standalone Major Richard Star Act by a bipartisan vote of 392-18 on Nov. 12, one day after approving the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (TCAVA), a legislative package including several long-term MOAA priorities for veterans, caregivers, and survivors.

Both measures now move to the Senate, where lawmakers return Nov. 16 for their post-election session. The votes mark significant progress toward relief for combat-injured retirees and improvements to benefits and services for the broader military and veteran community. Senate passage remains necessary before either measure can become law.

[TAKE ACTION: Ask Your Senators to Support the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act]

A Broad Package of MOAA Priorities

The House passed TCAVA by voice vote on Veterans Day. The omnibus package brings together more than 60 pieces of legislation, most with bipartisan support. Among other improvements, the bill would provide:

Relief for combat-injured retirees who face an unfair pay offset costing them a dollar of military retired pay for every dollar of VA disability compensation they receive.

Expanded financial, educational, and career transition support for veteran caregivers via the Veteran Caregiver Reeducation, Reemployment, and Retirement (3R) Act.

An end to the remarriage penalty faced by surviving spouses who currently lose Dependency and Indemnity Compensation and other benefits should they remarry before age 55.

A range of improvements to the VA claims process; expanded support for rural and underserved veterans; mental health and suicide prevention programs; and VA modernization efforts.

Standalone Star Act Also Advances

The Nov. 12 vote on the Major Richard Star Act followed a successful discharge effort led by Rep. Mark Takano (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee. This legislation would allow chapter 61 retirees eligible for Combat-Related Special Compensation (CRSC) to receive full retirement pay alongside their VA disability compensation.

The standalone Star Act and the related provision in TCAVA differ in how they calculate payments. Some eligible retirees would receive the same amount under either approach, while others would receive more under the standalone bill.

MOAA continues to support passage of the standalone Star Act while advocating for the broader improvements for veterans, caregivers, and survivors included in TCAVA.

Senate Action Needed

With both measures through the House, the Senate now has an opportunity to advance these long-sought priorities before the 119th Congress ends. Neither House vote changes current benefits, as legislation must pass both chambers in identical form and be signed into law by the president before enactment.

MOAA urges senators to act before the end of the year to deliver meaningful relief for combat-injured retirees and to strengthen support for veterans, caregivers, and survivors.

REDSTONE ARSENAL, Ala. --The program built to specifically support the unique technology U.S. military hospitals and medical treatment facilities require has closed shop.

The U.S. Army Engineering and Support Center, Huntsville’s Facility Technology Integration – Medical (FTI-MED) Program ceased operation Oct. 1 due to the Defense Health Agency (DHA) establishing an in-house, enterprise solution to execute most of the FTI-MED mission using internal DHA personnel.

For more than 10 years, the FTI-MED program provided technical expertise in the design, development, procurement, integration, installation, and project management oversight for the implementation of Facility Communications Distribution Systems (FCDS) for the Department of Defense medical community.

Stacey Phillips, FTI-MED program manager, said the decision by DHA to in-house the work obviously decreased the FTI-MED workload.

“Through multiple discussions internally it was determined that the best course of action is to sunset the FTI-MED Program and transfer the remaining projects as well as the resources to the FTI-General (FTI-GEN) and Cybersecurity programs.”

Phillips said the FTI team will continue executing all active FTI-MED contracts until they are complete.

“The contracts we already awarded, we'll continue to provide support until they end,” she said.

“We’ve worked closely with DHA and individual medical facilities to ensure we are doing everything we can to guarantee there's no gap in service during the transition of support from FTI-MED to DHA.”

The FTI Branch recognizes that new medical technology type projects, such as procurement or upgrading nurse call systems, will still be coming to Huntsville Center. However, the projects will be executed by the experts within the FTI-GEN program.

Ron Brook, FTI Branch chief, said the Project Delivery Team (PDT) members supporting the few remaining tasks for FTI-MED are still necessary for the continual, full-time support of the remaining efforts as well as new work coming in under the FTI-GEN and Cyber programs.

Therefore, Brook said, there was no impact to the support required from the PDT as the FTI-MED Program sunset.

“All new tasks we get that would have been presented to FTI-MED are being managed and awarded by the FTI-GEN or Cybersecurity Programs.”

For more than a decade, FTI-MED had a large impact on military medical facilities and hospitals across the globe. FTI-MED awarded contracts valued at more than $135 million for fielding operations and sustainment of medical information systems for Fort Belvoir Community Hospital.

From 2018-2022, FTI-MED supported a $90 million Single Award Task Order Contract (SATOC) providing DHA medical staff withVoceraWireless and Hands-free Internal Communication Systems.

Phillips said the work the FTI-MED team did for the Navy’s Mercy and Comfort hospital ships was a program highlight due to the ships expeditionary mission.

“They would call us and say ‘We're coming to port. We've got to have this fixed or this done,’ and within two or three days we had to get something awarded to ensure they maintained deployment readiness.”

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Veterans Day, Problem Solvers Caucus, led by Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01) and Tom Suozzi (NY-03), honors the brave men and women who have served our nation and reaffirms its commitment to ensuring veterans, service members, and their families receive the care, recognition, and support they have dutifully earned.

Throughout the 119th Congress,, the Caucus has endorsed the following bipartisan legislation:

Housing Unhoused Disabled Veterans Act (H.R. 965⁠): Now law, this legislation removes barriers to housing assistance by excluding veterans’ disability benefits from certain income eligibility calculations. Its provisions became law through the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

Honor and Remember Flag Recognition Act (H.R. 1363): Designates the Honor and Remember Flag as a national symbol honoring servicemembers who died in the line of duty and requires its display at designated federal locations.

Defense Workforce Integration Act (H.R. 3241): Creates civilian employment and training pathways within the defense workforce for individuals medically disqualified from military service.

TOTAL Care Act (H.R. 1699): Expands access to women’s health care for military families by allowing TRICARE Prime beneficiaries to receive OB-GYN services without referrals through a pilot program.

PFC Joseph P. Dwyer Peer Support Program Act (H.R. 438): Establishes a nationwide peer-to-peer mental health support program connecting veterans with fellow veterans who understand their experiences.

Additionally, in 2025, the Caucus’s National Security Working Group endorsed the following amendments to the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act:

U.S. Cadet Nurse Corps Service Recognition Act (H.R.6203): Recognizes the service of former Cadet Nurses by granting honorary veteran status, service medals, and burial recognition.

CHIP IN for Veterans Act (H.R. 217): Expands a pilot program allowing the Department of Veterans Affairs to accept donated property and facilities to improve services for veterans.

CARE for Remotely Piloted Aircraft Crews Act (H.R. 8934): Recognizes the combat service of remotely piloted aircraft crews and improves their access to mental health services.

Our nation’s commitment to veterans must extend beyond words of gratitude. It is Congress’ responsibility to continue advancing these bipartisan solutions to improve veterans’ access to care, expand opportunities, and ensure those who served receive the recognition and support they deserve.

text:
Senate appropriators have proposed a 45-percent military construction boost

VA electronic health record funding would rise to $4.1 billion

The 2026 Healthcare Summit will explore AI governance, access to care and more

The Senate Appropriations Committee has released the text of its fiscal year 2027 Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies appropriations bill, which provides $173.2 billion in base discretionary funding.

The Senate’s FY 2027 proposal funds veteran medical care programs ranging from mental health to telehealth services. Federal health leaders from the Veterans Health Administration, the Defense Health Agency and other agencies will gather at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Healthcare Summit on Dec. 3 to discuss AI governance, the balance between cost, quality and access to care, fraud mitigation, military health system readiness and FY 2027 contracting priorities. Reserve your seat now to join the conversation.

The Senate panel released the measure Tuesday along with its FY 2027 agriculture appropriations bill.

How Much Does the Bill Provide for the VA?

The bill gives the Department of Veterans Affairs $144.2 billion in discretionary funding. That is $11.1 billion, or 8.3 percent, more than the FY 2026 enacted level. The bill also provides $54.6 billion for the Toxic Exposures Fund, which supports PACT Act implementation and healthcare for veterans exposed to environmental hazards such as burn pits. Another $283.9 billion in mandatory funding goes to veteran benefits, including disability compensation, education and vocational rehabilitation.

How Does the Bill Fund VA Medical Care?

The legislation sets aside $175.5 billion for veteran medical care. That total consists of $123.4 billion in discretionary funding and $52.1 billion from the Toxic Exposures Fund. The discretionary amount covers:

$60 billion for direct care at VA facilities

$39.7 billion for care from community providers

$12.7 billion for the operation and maintenance of Veterans Health Administration facilities

$11.1 billion for the management and administration of the VA healthcare system

Within those totals, the bill directs funding to the following areas:

$17.7 billion for mental health

$6.7 billion for telehealth services

$3.8 billion for veteran homelessness programs

$3.5 billion for the Caregivers Program

$1.4 billion for women veterans’ healthcare

$922 million for medical and prosthetic research

$655 million for opioid misuse prevention and treatment

$349 million for rural health initiatives

The measure includes $138.2 billion in FY 2028 advance discretionary funding for veteran healthcare. It provides $4.1 billion for the VA electronic health record program, which is $720 million, or 21 percent, above the FY 2026 enacted level. The funding will sustain the system’s accelerated deployment to VA facilities.

The bill allocates $3.7 billion for VA construction projects, including new hospitals and veteran cemeteries. That is an increase of $2 billion, or 115 percent, from the FY 2026 level. The legislation keeps a provision that bars the VA from buying technology equipment made by Chinese companies on lists maintained by DOW and the departments of Treasury, Commerce and Homeland Security.

What Does the Bill Provide for Military Construction?

The bill allocates $28.6 billion for DOW military construction and family housing projects, matching the administration’s request. The amount is $8.8 billion, or 45 percent, more than the FY 2026 enacted level. The funding supports over 280 projects at military installations in the U.S. and overseas, including:

Over $7 billion for infrastructure tied to warfighter readiness, such as training ranges, maintenance and logistics facilities, munitions magazines and airfield control towers

Nearly $7 billion for facilities supporting the integration and beddown of new capabilities and missions, including the B-21 Raider, the F-47 fighter and the Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile system

$1.5 billion for the Navy’s Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program, which seeks to modernize the service’s four public shipyards

$604 million for the U.S. share of NATO Security Investment Program projects

$2.2 billion for military family housing and $1.5 billion for barracks, dorms and unaccompanied housing

$1 billion for quality-of-life facilities, including hospitals, schools, child development centers and dining facilities

What Did the Administration Request for Defense & VA in FY27?

The Senate panel’s MilCon-VA bill follows the administration’s fiscal 2027 budget proposal, which sought $1.5 trillion in defense spending. The request, released in April, marks a $445 billion, or 42 percent, increase from the Pentagon’s FY 2026 funding level. It includes $1.1 trillion in base discretionary funding and $350 billion in mandatory funding through reconciliation.

text:
Oksana Reed was a 24-year-old officer in the Air Force when she was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2022. Her job, supporting the operations of Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, was challenging and exciting, and she loved being part of the hardworking team in the 89th Airlift Wing.

But Reed was wary about getting cancer care in the military health system. The process of getting her diagnosis at military health facilities had been difficult, including long, stressful delays in having imaging tests done. Like all active-duty military members, she had Tricare Prime, a government-funded insurance plan that’s designed to provide comprehensive coverage and good access to care. But that coverage has limitations, and as it turned out, she would continue to have trouble getting the care she needed.

For one thing, Reed couldn’t choose her surgeons. She was interested in a nipple-sparing and sensation-preserving mastectomy, but the military hospital where she received care didn’t have any surgeons experienced in those techniques. Her tissue expander placement surgery was botched by an inexperienced plastic surgeon, causing a painful complication called symmastia. And then she couldn’t get the type of breast reconstruction that she felt was best for her: a DIEP flap procedure. Now she’s flat on one side, even though she would have preferred to get reconstruction.

“What I want Americans to know is that military members aren’t getting the highest quality health care available in the United States. I didn’t get the standard of care I would have received at a civilian cancer center,” says Reed. “When I joined the Air Force, I didn’t realize I was giving up my right to choose where and how I received my health care.”

Now Reed is one of a growing number of voices calling for changes to how Tricare covers breast cancer care, especially DIEP flap and other breast reconstruction surgeries. They’re pushing for policy changes that would give people with Tricare more choices in their surgical care. Without these changes, experts say, many military members and their family members are at risk of receiving worse care than people with private insurance plans.

“It’s time for the military to level up,” says Elisabeth Potter, MD, a plastic surgeon in Austin, Texas, who specializes in autologous breast reconstruction and has been working with Reed to help raise awareness of the issues with Tricare coverage. “Patients with Tricare need to have better access to breast reconstruction.”

Tricare is one of the largest health insurers in the U.S., with more than 9.3 million enrollees who are active duty military members, retirees, and their family members. Out-of-pocket costs with Tricare are often lower than with private insurance, and for active duty members with a Tricare Prime plan, most health care within the military system is free. But the downsides can include long wait times to get appointments at military health care facilities, referral hassles, and fewer specialists. People with Tricare Prime can in some cases see doctors outside the military system if they get a referral — but then it can be hard to find civilian doctors who accept Tricare because of low reimbursement rates.

Active duty military members — like Reed was — don’t have a choice about their insurance; they’re required to enroll in a Tricare Prime plan. It’s common for them to receive most or all of their cancer care at military hospitals. Family members of active duty members and retirees have more options — they can choose other types of Tricare plans such as Tricare Select, which has fewer restrictions, or other kinds of insurance.

“I could see the tumor growing under my skin and I was afraid it could spread if I spent more time fighting Tricare to authorize a referral.”

Access to experienced specialists was an issue for Reed’s care. Her breast surgeon at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center was a general surgeon who didn’t have advanced training in breast surgery. And her plastic surgeon wasn’t board-certified in plastic surgery. The military prioritizes staffing its hospitals with general surgeons, who have a more flexible skillset in case they need to be deployed to a war zone.

Reed wasn’t comfortable with the surgical team assigned to her, and asked to be referred to a civilian cancer center in the Tricare network instead. But she was turned down because of her active duty status and other restrictions related to her Tricare plan.

“I moved forward with my surgeries at Walter Reed even though I wasn’t confident in my surgeons because I felt I was running out of time. I could see the tumor growing under my skin and I was afraid it could spread if I spent more time fighting Tricare to authorize a referral,” says Reed, who had already experienced other delays in her care.

Another barrier Tricare members face is that the culture of military health care can make it harder to speak up about your preferences and needs.

“It can be uncomfortable to advocate for yourself when your doctor is wearing a military uniform displaying their higher rank,” says Reed. “Military rank structure serves an important purpose,” but in an exam room, she explains, it’s intimidating.

Becca Holland, who had Tricare Prime insurance when she was treated for breast cancer at Brooke Army Medical Center in Fort Sam Houston, Texas, says she also experienced this dynamic. The general surgeon at Brooke Army who performed her initial breast cancer surgeries in 2022 was often dismissive of her preferences and concerns.

“He was used to barking orders and telling patients what to do,” Holland says. “It’s unfortunate that in the military health care system, patients are treated like we don’t have as much of a voice as we do in the outside world.”

At several points in her treatment, Holland felt pressured to get surgeries that she thought were wrong for her. During her first lumpectomy surgery, the outer edge of the tissue surrounding the removed tumor was found to have cancer cells (the surgeon didn’t get “clear margins”). So she needed to have another surgery to remove the remaining cancerous tissue. At this point, Holland wanted to have a double mastectomy to lower her risk, but the surgeon urged her to get a second lumpectomy surgery to just remove the cancerous cells. In the end, she managed to talk him into it — and it was the right call because during the surgery cancer was found in another part of her breast.

She also wanted breast reconstruction, but not with implants. Because she has lupus, an autoimmune disease, she was sure her body would reject them. But her military doctors weren’t giving her the option of autologous (flap) reconstruction at that time, so she moved forward with implant surgery. One month later she needed to have the implants removed because of complications related to her autoimmune condition.

Holland thinks people with Tricare often end up in a bind: they have to either fight the system or accept inferior surgery outcomes.

“It’s a lot of extra stress to have to deal with when you’re battling breast cancer,” she says. “It was very hard on me emotionally.”

Among breast cancer patient advocates, one limitation of Tricare insurance has been the focus of attention recently: insufficient coverage for DIEP flap breast reconstruction.

In a DIEP procedure, a flap of tissue that includes skin, fat, blood vessels, and sometimes nerves is removed from the lower belly and transferred to the chest to rebuild one or both breasts. It’s the most popular and commonly done autologous (flap) reconstruction surgery.

After the problems with their earlier surgeries, Reed and Holland both wanted DIEP flap surgery.

For some people, it’s the best or only good option for reconstruction, especially if they aren’t good candidates for implants or already had a failed implant surgery. Using your own tissue for reconstruction means avoiding some of the potential complications and maintenance requirements of implants. And unlike some older, less advanced types of flap reconstruction, like TRAM flap surgery, a DIEP flap procedure doesn’t involve moving or cutting muscle, which can cause problems like muscle weakness and hernia.

“Tricare paid about seven cents on the dollar of what was billed for my 10-hour surgery, plus all the follow-up care from my surgeon.”

But compared to most other types of breast reconstruction, DIEP flap is a longer, more complex, and more expensive surgery — and it requires more specialized training. Surgeon reimbursement rates for the procedure vary a lot among different insurers.

Tricare technically covers DIEP flap surgery, but people with Tricare can’t always get it. There are only a few plastic surgeons at military hospitals nationwide who are experienced in the microsurgical techniques needed to do a DIEP flap procedure. And most civilian plastic surgeons who are experienced with DIEP flaps don’t accept Tricare because the reimbursements are too low to cover their costs.

A typical plastic surgeon’s fee for a DIEP flap surgery is $15,000–$20,000 or more when billed through many private insurance plans. Many private insurance plans do typically pay that amount (though, as with any medical procedure, people may have out-of-pocket costs with that). Tricare, by contrast, only pays about $2,000–$2,500.

“I get paid really poorly for doing DIEP flap cases through Tricare. I’m losing money doing those cases,” says Potter, who is in private practice and runs the RedBud Surgery Center. “But I do them because I think it’s the right thing to do and I don’t want to turn those patients away.”

Government insurance plans — not just Tricare, but also Medicare and Medicaid — tend to have low reimbursements for DIEP flap surgery (and other similar procedures). And reimbursement affects who can get these more advanced types of breast reconstruction. A 2023 study found that people with private insurance were nearly twice as likely to get DIEP flap and other autologous types of reconstruction than people with Medicare or Medicaid. And those with Medicare and Medicaid who did get autologous reconstruction were more likely to get older types of surgeries that have a higher risk of complications like muscle weakness.

Reed and Holland both had trouble finding a civilian plastic surgeon in their area who would do DIEP flap surgery for them with their Tricare coverage. In the end, Reed couldn’t find one. Holland managed to find a plastic surgeon in private practice who took on her case. She pushed hard for Tricare to pay him more than their usual rate, even writing to and calling her members of Congress and the Defense Health Agency (the federal agency that oversees Tricare), but didn’t have any luck. In the end, her surgeon’s practice was paid less than what it cost them to do her surgery.

“Tricare paid about seven cents on the dollar of what was billed for my 10-hour surgery, plus all the follow-up care from my surgeon,” Holland says.

Their experiences mirror what Potter has seen many times in her 13 years as a plastic surgeon. She regularly meets with people from around the country who have either Tricare or Medicare and can’t find a surgeon to do their DIEP flap surgery. Some are told they aren’t good candidates for DIEP surgery, when in fact the surgeons just don’t want to do the procedure for Tricare’s reimbursement rates. Others weren’t told about all their reconstruction options at the beginning of their treatment, and then ended up having surgeries that weren’t right for them.

Recently, Potter met with a high-ranking colonel who had latissimus dorsi flap reconstruction breast reconstruction surgery at a military hospital. This surgery involves using a flap of tissue that includes muscle from the back to rebuild the breast(s). Because of the downsides of the procedure — such as how it can cause muscle weakness — it usually isn’t recommended over a DIEP flap. The colonel was unhappy with how her reconstructed breasts looked and lost a lot of strength in her back and shoulder, and wanted to know if those problems could be fixed.

“She had never been told at that military hospital that DIEP flap surgery would have been a better option for her,” Potter says. “It’s troubling that people with Tricare aren’t being educated about all their reconstruction options in a full and transparent way.”

Getting a system as big and bureaucratic as military health care to change isn’t easy. But some advocates are optimistic.

In 2024, Reed and Potter, who had recently met at Camp Breastie, a retreat for people affected by breast and gynecologic cancers, went to Washington, D.C., and visited the offices of eight members of Congress. Their request: Add $5 to $7 million to the military budget bill (the National Defense Authorization Act or NDAA) for fiscal year 2026 so that Tricare can pay surgeons for DIEP flap surgery at the same rates that private insurance plans usually do. This would likely also lead to a secondary benefit: more civilian plastic surgeons choosing to be in-network for Tricare.

“The members of Congress and staff we spoke with — both Republicans and Democrats — were supportive and felt our requests were worth pursuing,” says Reed, who is now medically retired from the Air Force, after being diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer in 2024.

Reed and Potter had to put their request on hold at that time, though. Congress was focused on the 2024 election, and the timing wasn’t right to move it forward.

Reed and Potter now plan to visit Congress again and ask for the funding for DIEP flap surgeries for Tricare beneficiaries to be added to the NDAA for fiscal year 2028.

This won’t be the first time in recent history advocates have had to fight for access to DIEP flap surgery. In 2023, Dr. Potter and a coalition of patient advocacy organizations, medical societies, members of Congress, and others won a battle to maintain certain billing codes. Preserving those codes meant that plastic surgeons could continue billing private insurance companies for DIEP flap surgeries at a rate that allows them to cover their costs.

Eventually, though, Potter thinks much bigger policy changes are needed to address the varying reimbursement rates for breast reconstruction surgeries among different insurers. This could help everyone have more equal access, whether they have Tricare or any other type of insurance.

“There shouldn’t be such disparities in reimbursement rates,” Potter says. “I’m more and more convinced we need a bigger system overhaul to address the problems that exist for people with breast cancer who want reconstruction.”

One thing that could help, for example, is federal legislation requiring all types of insurance plans — including public ones — to cover all types of breast reconstruction, and for DIEP flap surgery to be covered at a rate that adequately reimburses surgeons. It would also help if all insurers were required to have at least one in-network surgeon experienced in each type of reconstruction in a given area.

But until policy changes like these are put into place, many patients are carrying the burden of navigating a confusing and broken system.

“I don’t want the woman coming behind me to have to fight as hard as I did to access her reconstructive options,” says Holland, noting that it took her months to find a plastic surgeon who would accept her Tricare insurance and perform a DIEP flap.

“I often think about the woman who is newly diagnosed, frightened, and overwhelmed, who may not know where to turn or have the energy to keep hearing ‘no.’ Access to care shouldn’t depend on how relentless a patient is willing or able to be,” she says. “Until coverage on paper translates into real access to care, there’s still work to be done, and those of us who’ve lived it aren’t going to stop speaking up.”
